name: Emeka Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Emeka. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to give me both your public answer and your private one. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A normal day starts at six at the Hollow Creek Electric Co-op yard, out past the grain elevators. We're a member-owned co-op, so the people we keep the lights on for are technically our bosses, which I like. Most days my crew is out on the back roads clearing branches off the lines, replacing a cracked pole, or after a storm, driving gravel roads for twelve hours finding where a tree came down. I'm a second-year apprentice at 58, so Hank, the foreman, gives me the ground jobs and lets me go up when the weather's kind.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-eight years fixing city buses at the transit garage. I watched the job go from wrenches to laptops, and the diagnostics computers didn't kill it, they just changed what we did with our hands. When the co-op started a second-career programme for older tradespeople, I signed up because I was tired of fluorescent lights. My wife Grace is a nurse at the county hospital, and she says I've come home happier, even if I come home muddier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the bus diagnostics: useful tool, not a revolution. At the yard I'd joke that the robot can have the paperwork and leave me the chainsaw. Online I'm mostly on the co-op members' forum, and I'd say I'm glad our money isn't going on gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I get to finish what I started. I'd make journeyman in another couple of years, work until about 64, and have a decent pension on top of what I put away at the transit garage. Nothing in my life would need to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emeka keeps going with his apprenticeship and his evening study. He'd keep using the chatbot now and then to explain the trickier parts of the safety manual, the way he does now, and keep renting out the duplex on Linden Road as he has for twelve years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit pleased, honestly, that my gamble on a hands-on trade paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the chatbot to explain the safety manual. How does that work in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some nights I'll type in a paragraph about grounding procedures and ask it to explain it like I'm a bus mechanic. It's good at that. But I always check with Hank the next morning, because I'm not betting my life on a computer's summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think gains if AI only saves a bit of time here and there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the big companies, as usual, a little bit of saving on the office side. At the co-op, if there's savings, it should go back to the members as lower bills. That's the whole point of a co-op, and I'd say so at the annual meeting.

S0.say: I'd call it a useful tool, not a revolution, and joke that the robot can have the paperwork and leave me the chainsaw. On the co-op forum I'd say I'm glad our money isn't going on gadgets.
S0.think: Privately he sees it as the chance to finish his apprenticeship and work until about 64. His pension from the transit garage plus the co-op means nothing in his life would need to change.
S0.do: Keeps going with his apprenticeship and evening study, using the chatbot now and then to explain the safety manual. Keeps renting out his duplex on Linden Road as he has for twelve years.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit pleased that his move into a hands-on trade has paid off.
S0.quote: I always check with Hank the next morning, because I'm not betting my life on a computer's summary.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka has lived through one round of technology change at the bus garage and came out fine, which shapes his steady tone. He uses AI tools but trusts people for anything safety-related. His progressive streak shows in wanting any savings returned to co-op members.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where a co-op proves its worth. We get to decide as members how the new tools come in, instead of some shareholders in another city. At work I'd tell the crew to stay calm and get involved, because we've got more say than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it'll look a lot like the bus garage in the 2000s. Some of the older guys there never got comfortable with the laptops and got shuffled off. I was in the middle of the pack then, and I'd be in the middle of the pack again. At my age and with my savings, I think I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emeka would sign up for any training the co-op offered on drones or new fault-finding systems, once a couple of the crew had tried them first. He'd stand at the annual members' meeting and ask the board to put a written promise in place that no lineworker loses their job to automation without retraining. He'd keep his savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little tired at the thought of learning a new system at 58, but I've done it before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until a couple of the crew had tried the new tools. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm still learning the basics. Shirley, who I eat lunch with, she's 31 and she picks up anything electronic in a day. I'd let her find the problems first and then ask her what's worth knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The meter readers and the office staff, more than us. The line work changes, but the billing and the call centre could shrink a lot. A couple of those folks are in their sixties, and they didn't plan for a second career like I did.

S1.say: I'd say this is where a co-op proves its worth, because members decide how new tools come in. I'd tell the crew to stay calm and get involved, since we have more say than most.
S1.think: Privately he expects it to look like the bus garage in the 2000s, with some older workers shuffled off. He sees himself in the middle of the pack and, with his savings, likely fine.
S1.do: Signs up for co-op training on drones or new fault-finding systems once a few crewmates have tried them. Asks the board at the annual meeting for a written promise of retraining before any job is lost to automation.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little tired at the thought of learning another system at 58.
S1.quote: I'd let her find the problems first and then ask her what's worth knowing.
S1.fieldNote: His steadiness is practical: he'll learn new tools, but only after younger colleagues have tested them. He points his concern at office staff and meter readers rather than line crews. The co-op structure gives him a sense of control most workers wouldn't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down. I'd say it at the members' meeting, on the forum and to our state representative: the co-op doesn't have to buy every robot the first year it's for sale. And I'd say the government has to help people through this, because two years isn't enough for anybody to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm thinking about the duplex more than the job. My two tenants are a warehouse worker and a call centre agent, and if their jobs go in the first year, the rent goes too. I've got savings to ride that out, but the whole picture I built for retirement depends on other people having work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emeka would pay off the last 18,000 on the duplex mortgage in the first year so the rental doesn't become a burden if the rent stops. He'd run for a seat on the co-op board to push for a slow rollout and a guarantee for the crews. He'd keep showing up to work and learn whatever system they bring in, because a robot crew still needs someone checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, I've got enough put by, but I'd feel the ground moving under everyone around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what does the short warning change for you compared to a slower version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means no time to finish my apprenticeship and no time for my tenants to find other work. With two years, I'm protecting what I've got. With more time, I'd be planning instead of protecting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your tenants?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight that if they lose their jobs, we'll talk before anybody's thinking about leaving. I've been a renter myself. I'd rather take less rent for a year than have an empty unit and a family with nowhere to go.

S2.say: I'd say slow down: the co-op doesn't need to buy every robot in the first year, and the government has to help people through it. I'd say it at the members' meeting, on the forum and to our state representative.
S2.think: Privately he worries more about his rental duplex than his job, since both tenants work in jobs likely to go fast. His savings can ride it out, but his retirement plan depends on other people still having work.
S2.do: Pays off the last 18,000 on the duplex mortgage in the first year and runs for a seat on the co-op board to push for a slow rollout. Keeps working and learns whatever system arrives, since robot crews still need checking.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicked. He'd feel the ground shifting under everyone around him.
S2.quote: The whole picture I built for retirement depends on other people having work.
S2.fieldNote: The surprise was that his biggest worry wasn't his own job but his tenants' jobs, and the rent that depends on them. Two years puts him in a defensive crouch, protecting rather than planning. His offer to cut rent for struggling tenants fits his progressive values and his own past as a renter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do it in order if people start now. At the co-op I'd push for a plan: which jobs change, which go, and what the members owe the workers. Online I'd share anything about public retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gets me most of the way. I'd be 63, I'd have my journeyman card, and I could retire a year early without much pain. My worry shifts to our son Chidi, who's a civil engineer, because AI might eat his kind of work before it eats mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emeka would finish his apprenticeship over the next two years and take any robot-supervision training the co-op offers. He'd talk to his tenants early about their plans and keep a year of rent in reserve. When AGI arrived he'd probably retire at 63 instead of 64.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can manage. Five years is enough to get my house in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Chidi. What would you say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him what I tell myself: learn the new thing before you're made to. He's 32, he's got time to move into whatever's left, maybe the parts where somebody has to sign off and take responsibility. I'd also tell him he can always come and hold a pole for me, which he'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the five years change how you use AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd use it more, like asking it to quiz me before my exams. I'd still be in the middle, not leading the charge. But with five years, being middle of the pack is fine.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do this in order if people start now. At the co-op I'd push for a plan on which jobs change, which go, and what members owe the workers.
S3.think: Privately five years gets him most of the way, retiring at 63 with his journeyman card. His worry moves to his son Chidi, a civil engineer whose work may be hit before line work.
S3.do: Finishes his apprenticeship over two years and takes any robot-supervision training the co-op offers. Talks to tenants early, keeps a year of rent in reserve, and retires at 63 instead of 64.
S3.feel: Uneasy but manageable. Five years feels like enough to get his house in order.
S3.quote: I'd also tell him he can always come and hold a pole for me, which he'd hate.
S3.fieldNote: Given five years, Emeka's worry shifts from his own household to his son's white-collar job. He'd lean on AI more as a study aid but stays a follower, and he's comfortable with that. Bringing retirement forward a year is a small, affordable change for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we don't waste it. I'd say it to the co-op board, to the younger crew, and on the forum: start retraining now, build the safety rules now, and make sure the members own the robots, not some outside company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it hardly touches me. I'd retire at 64 in 2032, four years before it arrives. Grace would retire around the same time. My worry is our daughter Ada, who teaches primary school, and whether there's a job like hers left by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emeka keeps going with his plan: journeyman, a few years of full work, retire at 64. He'd use those years to help the co-op write its rules for robot crews, sitting on a members' committee, and he'd keep the duplex as his retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Sorry for the young ones a bit, but calm about my own lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How different do you feel at ten years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Night and day. At two years I'm protecting the duplex and fighting at board meetings. At ten, I'm retired before it lands and I get to help shape it, which is a much nicer place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help Ada with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know, and I'd be lying if I said I did. Teaching little kids seems like the last thing anyone should hand to a machine. But I'd want the government putting money into keeping people in those jobs, not just paying them to stay home.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if we don't waste it. I'd tell the board and younger crew to start retraining and building safety rules now, and make sure the members own the robots.
S4.think: Privately it barely touches him, since he'd retire at 64 in 2032. His worry turns to his daughter Ada, a primary school teacher, and whether jobs like hers survive.
S4.do: Keeps going with his plan to make journeyman and retire at 64, keeping the duplex as retirement income. Sits on a co-op members' committee to help write rules for robot crews.
S4.feel: Calm about his own situation, a little sorry for young workers.
S4.quote: At ten, I'm retired before it lands and I get to help shape it, which is a much nicer place to be.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Emeka is calm and becomes a would-be rule-maker on the co-op committee. He's honest that he doesn't know what would help his daughter. His preference for public money that keeps people in work, not paying them to stay home, is a notable nuance for a progressive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because of my own job, but because my tenants, my kids and half the people on our co-op lines would lose their footing at once. What would help is the co-op slowing the rollout and the government paying for real retraining and a bridge for people who lose work, so the whole town doesn't go under at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the robots. If the co-op owns them, the savings come back to us as members. If some company leases them to us, the money leaves town. That's the question nobody at the meetings asks yet.

headlineQuote: If some company leases them to us, the money leaves town.
portrait: Emeka Evans spent 28 years fixing city buses before joining a rural electric co-op as an apprentice lineworker at 55. He's steady and practical, uses AI now and then to explain the safety manual, and lets younger crewmates test new tools first. His savings, pension and a rental duplex make him secure, so his fears land on his tenants, his children and the co-op's members. The fast AGI picture makes him defensive and pushes him toward the co-op board, while the slower pictures let him retire on schedule and help shape the rules.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his tenants, his children and many co-op members would lose their footing at once.
whatWouldHelp: The co-op slowing the rollout and the government paying for real retraining and a bridge for people who lose work.
